1H (Number Theory)

Words: 164 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 164
1H OurBigBook.com
For an integral binary quadratic form [a,b,c]=ax2+bxy+cy2 with a>0 and D=b2−4ac<0, the reduced positive definite binary quadratic form convention is ∣b∣≤a≤c, with b≥0 on either boundary ∣b∣=a or a=c. Since ∣D∣=4ac−b2≥3a2, the enumeration of reduced binary quadratic forms for D=−23 has a≤23/3​<3. The integer b is odd. For a=1, only b=1 is retained and c=6; for a=2, both b=±1 give c=3. Thus the complete list is
x2+xy+6y2,2x2+xy+3y2,2x2−xy+3y2.​
(1)
A proper representation of a prime uses a primitive representing vector. Completing that vector to a matrix in SL2​(Z) transforms a representing form to [p,b,c], so its discriminant of a binary quadratic form gives b2≡−23(modp). Conversely, choose an odd b satisfying this congruence and put c=(b2+23)/(4p). This is integral, and [p,b,c] is positive definite and represents p at (1,0). This proves the discriminant criterion for prime representation by a binary quadratic form here.
For p=23, quadratic reciprocity gives (−23/p)=(p/23). Including the ramified prime, the answer is therefore
p=23orpmod23∈{1,2,3,4,6,8,9,12,13,16,18}.​
(2)
For example [23,23,6] supplies a proper representation of 23. Reduction transfers every such representation to one of the three displayed forms.

a OurBigBook.com
The planar Brouwer fixed-point theorem says that every continuous map from the closed disk D to itself has a fixed point. If a retraction r:D→∂D existed, x↦−r(x) would be a continuous self-map of D. At a fixed point x=−r(x), x lies on the boundary, where r(x)=x; this would give x=−x, impossible on the unit circle.
Conversely, suppose a continuous self-map f:D→D has no fixed point. For each x, take the ray starting at f(x) through x, and let r(x) be its exit point on ∂D. The denominator ∣x−f(x)∣ never vanishes, and solving the quadratic intersection with the circle shows that the exit point depends continuously on x. More explicitly, with v=x−f(x),
r(x)=f(x)+λ(x)v,λ(x)=∣v∣2−f(x)⋅v+(f(x)⋅v)2+(1−∣f(x)∣2)∣v∣2​​.
(3)
The ray exits beyond or at x, so λ≥1, and when x∈∂D its exit point is x. Hence r is a retraction. Nonexistence of a boundary retraction and the planar fixed-point theorem are equivalent.

z6−z5+2z2+6z+1=0,∣z∣≤5/6.​
(4)
This supplies the requested existence and even places a root strictly inside the unit disk.

3G (Geometry of Group Actions)

Words: 197 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 197
3G OurBigBook.com
Every discrete additive subgroup of R2 has the form Zv1​+⋯+Zvr​ for linearly independent vectors, with r=0,1, or 2. A full translation lattice has r=2, and conversely every such integer span is a discrete cocompact subgroup. This classifies planar lattices up to a choice of basis.
A frieze group is a discrete group of planar Euclidean isometries whose translation subgroup is infinite cyclic and has finite index. Consider the glide reflection g(x,y)=(x+1,−y). Its square is translation by (2,0), whereas every odd power reverses orientation. Therefore ⟨g⟩≅Z, but none of its translation elements generates the whole group: they form the index-two subgroup ⟨g2⟩.
To realize exactly this frieze group, repeat a small scalene triangular motif at the points (n,(−1)n), reflecting the motif when n is odd. Choose the motif with three distinct side lengths and no internal symmetry. The displayed pattern has glide reflection symmetry g and translation period 2, but no pure horizontal reflection or vertical mirror. Distinct side lengths force any symmetry to preserve corresponding vertices, which rules out extra motif permutations; the sequence of heights then leaves exactly the powers of g.

4G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 156 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 156
4G OurBigBook.com
For Shannon-Fano coding, order the symbols by decreasing probability and recursively split each current list into two contiguous groups with total probabilities as close as possible. Label the two branches 0 and 1; the path to a symbol is its prefix code word. Here the first split is {a} of weight .4 against {b,c,d} of weight .6. The latter splits into {b} and {c,d}, each of weight .3. One answer is
a:0,b:10,c:110,d:111.​
(5)
For Huffman coding, repeatedly merge the two least-probable nodes and then read the resulting binary tree from the root. Merge c,d to weight .3, merge this node with b to weight .6, and merge with a. The same displayed prefix code results. Its mean length is .4+2(.3)+3(.2)+3(.1)=1.9 bits per symbol​. Choices at ties and exchange of binary labels yield other equivalent codes. Huffman coding minimizes mean length among binary prefix codes; the top-down Shannon-Fano construction does not have that general optimality guarantee.

5J (Statistical Modelling)

Words: 171 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 171
5J OurBigBook.com
Under independent normal distributions, maximum likelihood estimation minimizes (yA​−α)2+(yB​−β)2+(yC​−γ)2 subject to α+β+γ=π. A Lagrange multiplier gives the same correction at every corner. Writing s=yA​+yB​+yC​, the interior estimates are
α=yA​+3π−s​,β​=yB​+3π−s​,γ​=yC​+3π−s​.​
(6)
The result is unchanged if the common variance is unknown, since profiling it still minimizes the residual sum of squares. If physical positivity of the three angles is imposed and this projection gives a negative component, the constrained estimate over the closed simplex is instead θi​=max(yi​−λ,0), with λ chosen to make the components sum to π. If only strictly nondegenerate triangles are admitted, a boundary optimum is merely an unattained likelihood supremum.
The normal-error model is a useful small-error approximation, but its unbounded tails assign positive probability to impossible measured angles. Periodicity or a measurement convention may matter for large errors, and equal variance and independence require experimental justification. The exact sum constraint on the true angles does not itself invalidate independence of three raw measurement errors. After imposing that constraint, however, the fitted-angle errors are correlated: the covariance of the interior estimator is σ2(I−11T/3).

The Ricker population map has equilibria N=0 and N=K. Since f′(N)=er(1−N/K)(1−rN/K), their linearization multipliers are
f′(0)=er>1,f′(K)=1−r.​
(7)
Thus extinction is unstable and the positive equilibrium is locally asymptotically stable for 0<r<2, becoming unstable for r>2.
To verify an actual period-doubling bifurcation, rather than only a multiplier crossing, put N/K=1+x and r=2+ε. The centered map is
x↦−(1+ε)x+O(εx2)+32​x3+O(εx3+x4).
(8)
Its second iterate minus x is 2εx−34​x3 to leading order. After rescaling x=ε​y, the limiting nonzero roots are simple, so the implicit function theorem continues them. Besides x=0, two nearby points therefore appear for ε>0, with x±​=±3ε/2​+O(ε). The map exchanges these points, and the derivative of its second iterate there is 1−4ε+O(ε3/2), so the emerging two-cycle is attracting. The bifurcation at r=2 is supercritical period doubling.
For nonnegative populations, f increases up to N=K/r and decreases thereafter to zero. Hence every update after the initial time satisfies
0≤Nt​≤f(K/r)=rK​er−1,t≥1.​
(9)
The bound is attained by choosing N0​=K/r; it is not a bound on an arbitrary initial population.

At a stationary bifurcation, a real eigenvalue of the equilibrium linearization crosses zero; the critical motion has zero frequency. At a Hopf bifurcation, a conjugate pair crosses the imaginary axis at ±iω with ω>0, permitting a nearby limit cycle.
The Hopf normal form has a small cycle when R2=μ/a+O(μ2)>0. Its radial multiplier exponent is ∂r​r˙∣R​=−2μ+O(μ2), while the origin's radial exponent is μ. Thus: for μ<0<a, there is an attracting spiral and no small cycle; for 0<μ,a, a repelling spiral is surrounded by an attracting cycle; for μ,a<0, an attracting spiral is surrounded by a repelling cycle; for a<0<μ, there is a repelling spiral and no small cycle. Outside the repelling cycle in the third case the local radial flow points outward; a cubic normal form makes no global prediction about where it goes.
The subcritical bifurcation has a<0 and the unstable radius branch R=μ/a​+O(∣μ∣3/2) on μ<0, meeting the origin at μ=0. On either existing branch, the angular speed is ω+(c−b/a)μ+O(μ2), so
T=ω+(c−b/a)μ+O(μ2)2π​,dμdT​=−ω22π​(c−ab​)+O(μ).​
(10)

8C OurBigBook.com
For the beta function, split 1=t+(1−t) inside the integral to obtain B(z,q)=B(z,q+1)+B(z+1,q). Integrating the derivative of tq(1−t)z over (0,1) gives qB(z+1,q)=zB(z,q+1), since both endpoint terms vanish in the initial domain. Combining these identities yields
B(z,q)=zz+q​B(z+1,q).​
(11)
Repeatedly apply this recurrence until Re(z+n)>0. Each resulting expression agrees with the original integral on overlap, so it gives its unique analytic continuation. Possible singularities are only z=0,−1,−2,….
Near z=0, zB(z,q)→qB(1,q)=1. Continuing the recurrence downwards gives
Resz=−n​B(z,q)=n!(−1)n​(q−1)(q−2)⋯(q−n),n≥0,​
(12)
where the empty product is 1. The recurrence shows that each singularity is at most a simple pole. If q is not a positive integer, all these residues are nonzero and all the listed points are poles. If q=m is a positive integer, poles occur only for 0≤n<m; the later candidates are removable, as is also clear from B(z,m)=(m−1)!/[z(z+1)⋯(z+m−1)]. This qualification matters when claiming a pole at every nonpositive integer.

mi​a2θ¨i​=k(θi+1​−2θi​+θi−1​).​

All successive angular gaps are 2π/N in equilibrium, so their two contributions cancel. Because the potential depends only on gaps, a uniform change of all angles costs no energy. Its Hessian therefore annihilates (1,…,1), giving a zero-frequency normal mode. The corresponding motion is rigid rotation, θi​(t)=θi(0)​+A+Bt, including a constant common angular shift.
For two particles write θ2​−θ1​=π+δ2​−δ1​. Both cyclic gaps contribute, so the quadratic potential is k(δ2​−δ1​)2. With the specified masses, the mass matrix is kmdiag(1,2) and the stiffness matrix is 2k(1−1​−11​). The generalized eigenvalue problem gives
ω0​=0,(δ1​,δ2​)∝(1,1);ω1​=3/m​,(δ1​,δ2​)∝(2,−1).​

The finite-frequency normal mode keeps the mass-weighted mean angle fixed and changes the angular separation sinusoidally. Together with the two rigid-rotation constants, it spans all small motions about equilibrium.

For a regular spherical star, mass conservation gives m′=4πr2ρ. Multiplying the hydrostatic equilibrium equation by r2/ρ and differentiating therefore yields
drd​(ρr2​drdP​)=−4πGr2ρ.​
(15)
At the center, finite density implies m(r)=O(r3), so a regular pressure satisfies P(0)=Pc​<∞ and P′(0)=0. At a free outer boundary in vacuum, P(R)=0; a surrounding medium would instead prescribe its external pressure.
Differentiate the auxiliary function, using both equations:
F′=−r2Gmρ​+4πr4Gmm′​−2πr5Gm2​=−2πr5Gm2​<0

Pc​>8πR4GM2​.​

Let 1 be the constant function and define h=L1∈C([0,1]). Positivity gives h≥0. Fix any x and any continuous f. The function g=f−f(x)1 vanishes at x, so the zero-preserving assumption gives Lg(x)=0. By linearity this is Lf(x)−f(x)L1(x)=0. Since x was arbitrary,
Lf=hffor every f∈C([0,1]),h=L1≥0.​
(18)
This proves the zero-preserving linear operator on continuous functions representation. Zero preservation and linearity determine the multiplication operator; positivity is needed only for the multiplier's sign. The three numbered conditions in the source are hypotheses of this one request, rather than three separate subquestions.

12G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 244 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 244
12G OurBigBook.com
In the Rabin cryptosystem, choose distinct large odd primes p,q, publish N=pq, and encrypt m as c=m2modN. Usually p,q≡3(mod4), so a square root modulo each prime is obtained by exponentiating to (p+1)/4 or (q+1)/4. Combine the two independent choices of signs by the Chinese remainder theorem to obtain the four roots modulo N for a message coprime to N. Redundancy or a specified encoding distinguishes the intended message. Factoring N makes decryption easy; a general square-root oracle conversely factors N by obtaining two roots not congruent up to sign and taking their greatest common divisor with N.
For the Repeated-message attack on the Rabin cryptosystem, first compute d=gcd(N,N′). If d=1, use the two ciphertexts to reconstruct s∈[0,NN′) with s≡m2(modN) and s≡m2(modN′). Since 0<m<min(N,N′), we have m2<NN′, so this reconstruction is the ordinary integer m2. Therefore
m=s​.​
(19)
If distinct semiprime moduli have d>1, they share a prime; the gcd instead exposes their factors, allowing ordinary Rabin decryption with the usual encoding check. The two cases cover the stated protocol with distinct standard moduli.
In the coprime case, learning this message does not normally reveal the factors or a decryption key, so other messages encrypted only once remain protected by the square-root problem. Exceptional messages with gcd(m,N)>1 do reveal a factor, and the shared-prime-modulus case compromises other messages too. Repetition under fresh coprime moduli is the vulnerability used here, rather than a universal attack on every ciphertext.

f′(0)=−r<0,f′(r)=r(1−r)>0,f′(1)=−(1−r)<0.​

There is a branch-phase discrepancy in the printed identity. Set K(z)=∫−11​et(1−t2)zdt using the positive real base. Shrink the anticlockwise loop at 1. The outward interval carries phase e−iπz and its return phase eiπz; their difference gives −2isin(πz)∫01​et(1−t2)zdt. The clockwise loop at −1 starts with phase eiπz and returns with e−iπz, giving the same coefficient on (−1,0). Small endpoint circles vanish for Rez>−1. Thus the branch phase in a figure-eight analytic continuation integral is
J(z)=−2isin(πz)K(z).​
(27)
If the printed interval integral uses the prescribed argument −π, then I(z)=e−iπzK(z), and the corrected formula is instead
J(z)=−2ieiπzsin(πz)I(z).​
(28)
For example at z=1/2, K>0, I=−iK and J=−2iK; the printed right side without the phase would be the real number −2K. Interpreting its interval integrand as (1−t2)z restores the intended identity.
On the fixed contour away from its branch points, the continued logarithm is bounded and etexp[zlog(t2−1)] is entire in z, uniformly on compact sets. Hence J is an entire function. Division by the sine gives a meromorphic continuation of K, and multiplication by e−iπz gives the continuation of the specified I. The only candidate singularities are integers, at most simple. All 0,1,2,… are removable because the interval integral is already holomorphic on Rez>−1.
The negative integers z=−n, n≥1, are genuine simple poles. At such a point the contour integrand is single-valued and
J(−n)=2πi[Rest=1​(t2−1)net​−Rest=−1​(t2−1)net​].
(29)
The first residue is e times a rational number. The second is e−1 times a nonzero rational number: expand es(−2+s)−n at s=0, whose degree-n−1 coefficient has sign (−1)n and nonzero magnitude. They cannot be equal because e2 is irrational. Therefore J(−n)=0, and the simple sine zero creates a simple pole. In particular Resz=−n​K=−J(−n)/[2πi(−1)n].
A circle enclosing both branch points has total logarithmic change 4πi, rather than zero as for the figure eight. For a circle based at t=2 with initial real logarithm, shrinking it leaves a connector from 1 to 2 as well as the two banks of the interval. Explicitly its integral is
JC​(z)=2ie2πizsin(πz)K(z)+(e4πiz−1)∫12​et(t2−1)zdt.
(30)
Thus it is not just a known sine factor times K: an additional endpoint-singular integral remains. The figure-eight contour eliminates precisely that connector term. This explains why replacing it by the large circle does not give the same direct continuation method.

The Godel completeness theorem for first-order logic states that Γ⊨ϕ implies Γ⊢ϕ; together with soundness, semantic consequence and derivability coincide. Equivalently, every syntactically consistent first-order theory has a model. The compactness theorem states that a set of first-order sentences has a model if and only if every finite subset has a model. These statements use nonempty first-order structures.

For each n, let σn​ assert the existence of n distinct elements. If a theory T has arbitrarily large finite models, every finite subset of T∪{σn​:n≥1} has a model. By the compactness theorem, this extended theory has a model, necessarily infinite. Since fields of size 2j are arbitrarily large, no first-order theory can have exactly the finite fields of characteristic two as its models.
Suppose instead a finite conjunction χ axiomatized exactly the infinite fields of characteristic two. Let T2​ be the field axioms with 1+1=0. Then T2​∪{¬χ} would have exactly the finite characteristic-two fields as models, contradicting the preceding conclusion. Equivalently, compactness of T2​∪{σn​}⊨χ would force some finite size threshold, but arbitrarily large finite fields still fail χ. The infinite characteristic-two fields are not finitely axiomatizable.

The intended closed-term witness property for quantifier-free existential sentences needs at least one closed term. Under this hypothesis, suppose the set Γ={¬ϕ(t):t a closed term} were consistent. By the Godel completeness theorem, it has a model M. Take the substructure M0​ whose elements are the interpretations of closed terms. It is nonempty and closed under every function symbol. Atomic formulas and their negations have the same truth values in M0​ as in M, and induction extends this to every quantifier-free formula.
The provable sentence ∃xϕ(x) is true in M0​ by soundness. Its witness is tM0​ for some closed term t, so M⊨ϕ(t), contradicting M⊨Γ. Hence Γ is inconsistent. The compactness theorem gives a finite inconsistent subset, so completeness and classical propositional reasoning yield
⊢ϕ(t1​)∨⋯∨ϕ(tn​).​
(35)
Without a constant or nullary function, the printed assertion is false as written: in the equality-only language there are no closed terms, but ∃x(x=x) is provable. Then Γ is empty and consistent. One may repair the usual theorem by assuming a nonempty set of closed terms or adjoining a fresh constant; the latter proves a witness disjunction in the enlarged language, not the missing closed terms in the original one.

Here graphs are finite and simple. To prove Dirac theorem, take a longest path v1​,…,vℓ​. All neighbours of either endpoint lie on the path. Among indices 1≤i<ℓ, let S={i:v1​vi+1​ is an edge} and T={i:vi​vℓ​ is an edge}. Since ∣S∣+∣T∣=d(v1​)+d(vℓ​)≥n>ℓ−1, some i lies in both. Following the path forward to vi​, jumping to vℓ​, and following it backwards to vi+1​ closes a cycle containing every vertex of the path. The degree condition makes the graph connected: two components would each have at least δ+1>n/2 vertices. If ℓ<n, connectedness gives an edge from an outside vertex to the cycle, and breaking the cycle there makes a longer path. This contradiction proves a Hamiltonian cycle.
For even n=2m, the complete bipartite graph Km−1,m+1​ has minimum degree m−1 and no Hamiltonian cycle. For odd n=2m+1, Km,m+1​ has minimum degree m and likewise fails: a bipartite cycle uses equal numbers from its two parts. These examples include the smallest applicable n.
Adding one universal vertex gives n+1 vertices and minimum degree at least (n+1)/2 when the original minimum degree is at least (n−1)/2. Apply the proved theorem and remove the universal vertex from its cycle. The remaining sequence is a Hamiltonian path in the original graph.
A necessary condition for a Hamiltonian cycle is that deleting a nonempty vertex set S leaves at most ∣S∣ components, since deleting those vertices breaks a spanning cycle into at most that many path pieces. For any k≥1, take the connected star G=K1,k+2​. In Gk​, deleting its center and the k new vertices leaves k+2 components, more than k+1. Even two-connectivity does not suffice: take G=K2,k+3​, which is two-connected. Deleting its two-vertex part and the k new vertices from Gk​ leaves k+3 components, more than k+2. Both connectivity requirements admit counterexamples for every k.

The Uniform boundedness principle states that a pointwise bounded family T of bounded linear maps from a Banach space X to a normed space Y is uniformly bounded in operator norm. Define closed sets En​={x:supT∈T​∥Tx∥≤n}. Pointwise boundedness makes their union X. The Baire category theorem gives a ball B(x0​,r)⊂En​ for some n. For ∥v∥<r, both x0​+v and x0​ lie in En​, so ∥Tv∥≤2n for every T. Scaling yields supT​∥T∥≤2n/r, proving the principle.
For the separately continuous bilinear map, consider Tx​(y)=F(x,y) with ∥x∥≤1. Each Tx​ is bounded and linear. For fixed y, continuity of the other linear map gives sup∥x∥≤1​∥F(x,y)∥<∞. Apply the Uniform boundedness principle to this family to get
∥F(x,y)∥≤M∥x∥∥y∥.​

For the trilinear map, fix w. The just-proved bilinear result bounds G(⋅,⋅,w). Thus the bounded linear maps Tx,y​:w↦G(x,y,w), for ∥x∥,∥y∥≤1, are pointwise bounded. Apply the Uniform boundedness principle once more to obtain ∥G(x,y,w)∥≤C∥x∥∥y∥∥w∥. Expansion of the difference in three slots proves joint continuity. Separate continuity suffices for these multilinear maps.
Without linearity it does not suffice. On R2 set H(x,y)=xy/(x2+y2) away from the origin and H(0,0)=0. Each coordinate section is continuous, but H(t,t)=1/2 for t=0, so H is not continuous at the origin.

A divisor on a compact connected Riemann surface is a finite formal sum D=∑p​np​p with integer coefficients; its degree is ∑p​np​. A canonical divisor is the divisor of zeros and poles of a nonzero meromorphic differential. Two divisors are linearly equivalent when their difference is the divisor of a nonzero meromorphic function. Such principal divisors have degree zero, but equal degree does not generally imply linear equivalence of divisors.
For example take distinct points p,q on a genus-one surface. If p−q were principal, its function would define a degree-one meromorphic map to the sphere, since it has just one simple pole. A degree-one map between compact Riemann surfaces is a biholomorphism, contradicting their different genera. Thus these degree-one divisors are not equivalent.
Define L(D)={f meromorphic:(f)+D≥0}∪{0} and ℓ(D)=dimC​L(D). The Riemann-Roch theorem states
ℓ(D)−ℓ(K−D)=degD+1−g.
(47)
Since all holomorphic functions on the compact surface are constant, ℓ(0)=1. Setting D=0 gives ℓ(K)=g. Multiplication by a fixed meromorphic differential identifies L(K) with holomorphic differentials, so their dimension is g. Setting D=K then gives
dimH0(S,Ω1)=g,degK=2g−2.​
(48)
For g=2, choose a nonzero holomorphic differential, whose effective canonical divisor has degree two. Since ℓ(K)=2, L(K) contains a nonconstant meromorphic function. Its pole divisor is bounded by that effective K, proving existence of a nonconstant function with total pole multiplicity at most two.

cα+β=1+∫ϕ(x)[cp0​(x)−p1​(x)]dx.

Pointwise minimization over 0≤ϕ≤1 forces rejection where p1​>cp0​ and acceptance where p1​<cp0​, with arbitrary randomization on equality. Conversely those choices minimize every integrand. The equivalence holds almost everywhere, since changing a test on a common null set cannot change its errors. With both weights strictly positive, any simultaneous improvement of the two errors, strict in at least one, would lower this weighted sum. Every such positive-threshold likelihood ratio test is admissible for the two simple hypotheses.
For the specified densities the likelihood ratio is
Rθ​(x)=⎩⎨⎧​0,x(1−θ)2x−θ​,​0<x<θ,θ≤x≤1.​

Threshold zero rejects everywhere above θ and permits arbitrary rejection below θ, where both weighted choices tie; values at individual endpoints do not affect errors. These describe all nonnegative-threshold likelihood ratio tests, including their limiting accept-all and reject-all cases.
The upper-tail test ϕk​ has size 1−k2. If θ<k, it is a positive-threshold likelihood ratio test and is admissible. If θ=k, it rejects exactly the alternative's support, with power one; no test can retain power one with smaller size, so it remains admissible. If θ>k, it still has power one but wastes rejection probability on (k,θ), where the alternative density vanishes. The test ϕθ​ has the same power and smaller size, so
ϕk​ is admissible against fixed θ⟺θ≤k.​

Nevertheless ϕk​ is a uniformly most powerful test at size 1−k2 against all 0<θ<1: for θ<k, apply the Neyman-Pearson lemma; for θ≥k, its power is already the maximum one. It is also admissible against the composite alternative. Indeed choose any 0<θ<k. Strict monotonicity of its likelihood ratio makes ϕk​ the unique positive-threshold minimizer up to null sets. A test dominating it for the composite problem would either improve the weighted simple risk at this θ, impossible, or tie that risk and coincide almost everywhere. Since p0​>0 throughout (0,1), such coincidence also precludes improvement at any other θ.

Y is a supermartingale⟺μ≤0,Y is a martingale⟺μ=0.​

μ=rE​−rD​under QE​.​

For a Dollar investor, the Euro bank account has Dollar value erE​t/Yt​. After Dollar discounting, it is e(rE​−rD​)t/Yt​. Its conditional mean growth exponent is rE​−rD​+σ2−μ, so the martingale requirement gives
μ=rE​−rD​+σ2under QD​.​

29I (Optimization and Control)

Words: 240 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 240
29I OurBigBook.com
The average-cost Bellman equation is
g+θ(x)=a∈Ainf​[c(x,a)+y∑​pxy​(a)θ(y)].​
(70)
If a constant g and bounded relative cost function θ solve this equation and a stationary control attains the infimum in each state, that control is optimal and its long-run expected average cost is g. Indeed the Bellman inequality telescopes along any controlled trajectory; dividing by the number of steps removes the bounded endpoint terms and gives a lower bound g. The attaining policy makes the inequalities equalities. An unbounded θ requires the corresponding endpoint/transversality justification, which the question permits for this example.
To maximize occupation of zero, minimize c(x,u)=−1{x=0}​ and try θ(x)=μ∣x∣ with μ>0. For x>0, the expected increment of θ is μ(2u−1), minimized at u=α; for x<0, it is μ(1−2u), minimized at u=1−α. At zero its expected next value is μ, independent of u. Thus g=μ(2α−1) away from zero and g=−1+μ at zero. Solving gives
μ=2(1−α)1​,g=−2(1−α)1−2α​,πmax​=−g=2(1−α)1−2α​.​
(71)
An optimal control always biases a nonzero position towards zero: u=α on positive integers, u=1−α on negative integers, and any allowed u at zero.
As an independent occupation check, fix the choice u0​ at zero. The stationary positive tail begins at π1​=π0​u0​/(1−α) and has common ratio α/(1−α); the negative tail begins at π−1​=π0​(1−u0​)/(1−α) with the same ratio. Summing these geometric tails gives 1=π0​[1+1/(1−2α)], reproducing the boxed optimum. The chain has period two, but its time-averaged occupation still converges to this stationary proportion.

i OurBigBook.com
A fundamental solution of a linear differential operator P(D) is a distribution E satisfying P(D)E=δ0​. For the three-dimensional negative Laplacian,
E(x)=4π∣x∣1​,−ΔE=δ0​.​
(72)
Away from zero the function is harmonic. For a test function ϕ, integrate E(−Δϕ) outside a ball of radius ε and use Green's identity. The small inner sphere contributes ϕ(0)+o(1) because the normal derivative of E has total outward-from-the-ball flux −1; the other boundary term is O(ε). Letting ε→0 verifies the distributional equation and its normalization.

ii

Words: 99 Articles: 1

Solution

ii OurBigBook.com
The mean value property for harmonic functions states that if u is harmonic on a neighborhood of a closed ball, then its average on the ball or its boundary sphere equals its value at the center. To prove it in three dimensions, define M(r)=(4π)−1∫S2​u(x+rω)dω. Differentiation and the divergence theorem give
M′(r)=4πr21​∫∂B(x,r)​∂n​udS=4πr21​∫B(x,r)​Δudy=0.
(73)
Since M(r)→u(x) as r→0, the spherical average equals u(x). Integrating 4πr2M(r) from zero to the ball radius gives the volume version,
u(x)=∣B(x,R)∣1​∫B(x,R)​u(y)dy.​
(74)
For balls merely contained in the open harmonicity domain, apply the result first to smaller radii and pass to the radius of interest by continuity.

iii OurBigBook.com
Apply the volume mean value property to the two balls and use nonnegativity together with inclusion:
u(w)=∣B(w,R)∣1​∫B(w,R)​u≥∣B(w,R)∣1​∫B(z,r)​u=(Rr​)3u(z).​
(75)
For any w,z∈B(x,r), the triangle inequality gives B(z,r)⊂B(w,3r)⊂B(x,4r)⊂Ω. Taking R=3r in the previous bound therefore gives u(w)≥u(z)/27. Take the infimum over w and supremum over z to obtain
B(x,r)inf​u≥3−3B(x,r)sup​u.​
(76)
No positivity stronger than nonnegativity is needed; if a value vanishes, this argument forces every value in the smaller ball to vanish too.

31C (Integrable Systems)

Words: 263 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 263
31C OurBigBook.com
Use the rapidly decaying real-potential normalization ut​−6uux​+uxxx​=0. Let D=∂x​, L=−D2+u and A=4D3−3(uD+Du)=4D3−6uD−3ux​. Expanding the commutator cancels its derivative terms and gives
[L,A]=6uux​−uxxx​,Lt​=[L,A].​
(77)
Thus the KdV equation is the compatibility condition of the Lax pair Lψ=λψ, ψt​=−Aψ. The operator A is skew-adjoint on decaying functions. Its evolution transports normalized eigenfunctions unitarily, so the spectrum of L is fixed; alternatively differentiating Lψ=λψ and using the two equations gives λt​ψ=0.
At each time solve the KdV Schrodinger spectral problem. For λ=k2>0, use the left Jost solution f−​, normalized as e−ikx at x→−∞, and write f−​∼a(k,t)e−ikx+b(k,t)eikx at +∞. The right reflection coefficient is R=b/a, and transmission is 1/a. Because −A tends to −4D3 at infinity, maintaining this Jost normalization gives f−,t​=−Af−​+4ik3f−​. Substitution of its two asymptotic waves yields at​=0 and bt​=8ik3b. The negative discrete eigenvalues are −κj2​, fixed in time. A unit-normalized bound state with right tail cj​(t)e−κj​x obeys cj′​=4κj3​cj​. Consequently the Time evolution of KdV scattering data is
R(k,t)=R(k,0)e8ik3t,κj​(t)=κj​(0),cj​(t)=cj​(0)e4κj3​t.​
(78)
These signs follow from the specified right-reflection convention; reversing which infinity defines reflection reverses the continuous-data phase convention.
The inverse scattering transform now solves the nonlinear evolution in three steps. Compute R(k,0), the discrete eigenvalues and the norming constants from u(x,0); evolve this KdV scattering data by the simple formulas above; reconstruct u by the Gelfand-Levitan-Marchenko equation. Explicitly set
F(s,t)=2π1​∫R​R(k,t)eiksdk+∑j​cj​(t)2e−κj​s
(79)
and solve, for y≥x,
K(x,y,t)+F(x+y,t)+∫x∞​K(x,z,t)F(z+y,t)dz=0.
(80)
The recovered potential is u(x,t)=−2dK(x,x,t)/dx​. Each fixed discrete eigenvalue produces a soliton component, whereas the continuous scattering data encode the dispersive part. The inverse transform, rather than a linear superposition of the potentials, accounts for their nonlinear interaction.

Let H∣n⟩=En​∣n⟩, with nondegenerate eigenvalues, and expand the perturbed state as ∣n⟩+λ∣n(1)⟩+⋯, choosing ⟨n∣n(1)⟩=0. The first-order eigenvalue equation gives En(1)​=Vnn​ and, after projection onto m=n, ⟨m∣n(1)⟩=Vmn​/(En​−Em​). Projecting the second-order equation onto n then gives the second-order nondegenerate perturbation theory result
En​(λ)=En​+λVnn​+λ2m=n∑​En​−Em​∣Vmn​∣2​+O(λ3).​
(81)
For angular momentum, j=0,1/2,1,…, m=−j,−j+1,…,j, and J2∣jm⟩=j(j+1)∣jm⟩, J3​∣jm⟩=m∣jm⟩ in units ℏ=1.
Take H0​=−γB3​J3​ with γB3​=0 and perturbation −γB1​J1​. The diagonal matrix element of J1​=(J+​+J−​)/2 vanishes. Only m±1 contribute at second order. Their squared matrix elements are [j(j+1)−m(m±1)]/4, and their unperturbed energy denominators are respectively γB3​ and −γB3​. Thus
ΔEm(2)​=4B3​γB12​​{[j(j+1)−m(m+1)]−[j(j+1)−m(m−1)]}=−2B3​γmB12​​.
(82)
Hence Em​=−γB3​m−γmB12​/(2B3​)+O(B14​)​. Rotating the quantization axis to the field gives exact energies −γmB​B32​+B12​​. Labeling each branch continuously from its original m gives Em​=−γmB3​1+B12​/B32​​, whose expansion agrees, including negative B3​. If B3​=0, the nondegenerate starting point fails and this expansion cannot be used.

33E (Applications of Quantum Mechanics)

Words: 191 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 191
33E OurBigBook.com
For an electron of charge −e, magnetic minimal coupling gives H=(p+eA)2/(2m). In Landau gauge, A=(0,Bx,0), and fixing the conserved py​ turns the Hamiltonian into a harmonic oscillator centered at x=−py​/(eB). The Landau levels are therefore
En​=ℏωc​(n+21​),ωc​=eB/m,n=0,1,2,….​
(83)
In a rectangle of dimensions Lx​,Ly​, consecutive momenta differ by 2πℏ/Ly​, so consecutive oscillator centers differ by 2πℏ/(eBLy​). Centers lying in the sample supply eBA/(2πℏ) orbitals per level. Neglecting the spin-field interaction leaves two degenerate spin states, rather than removing spin from Pauli counting. Thus each level holds D=eBA/(πℏ) electrons, to leading order for a large sample.
In the specified field range, N≤D≤2N. At zero temperature fill the lowest level with D electrons and the next with 2N−D. This ground-state filling of two spin-degenerate Landau levels gives
Etotal​=mℏeB​(3N−D)=m3NℏeB​−πme2AB2​.​
(84)
At the lower endpoint the first two levels are exactly full; at the upper endpoint only the lowest level is full. Both give
Eendpoints​=mA2πℏ2N2​.​
(85)
Between them the total energy is a concave quadratic and is larger than this common endpoint value. Filling reorganizes as the magnetic degeneracy increases; ignoring spin splitting still requires retaining the twofold spin degeneracy in this calculation.

⟨(E−⟨E⟩)2⟩=kB​T2CV​.​
(86)
Differentiating ⟨E2⟩−⟨E⟩2 with the same rule gives minus ⟨E3⟩−3⟨E⟩⟨E2⟩+2⟨E⟩3, namely minus the third central moment. Thus
⟨(E−⟨E⟩)3⟩=kB2​[T4(∂T∂CV​​)V​+2T3CV​].​
(87)
These identities exhibit the second and third energy cumulants as successive derivatives of logZ.
For the monatomic ideal gas, ⟨E⟩=3NkB​T/2, CV​=3NkB​/2 and ∂T​CV​=0. The variance is 3N(kB​T)2/2 and the third central moment is 3N(kB​T)3. Division by the corresponding mean-energy powers gives

35E (General Relativity)

Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 133
35E OurBigBook.com
An affinely parametrized geodesic satisfies d2xa/dλ2+Γabc​TbTc=0, which is exactly ∇T​T=0. The Levi-Civita connection is metric-compatible, so
dλd​g(X,Y)=(∇T​g)(X,Y)+g(∇T​X,Y)+g(X,∇T​Y)=0
(89)
when both vectors are parallel transported. Their inner product is constant, including their lengths; this preservation in fact holds along any path with parallel vectors, not only a geodesic.
For the two-parameter family, mixed partial derivatives commute and Γabc​ is symmetric in its lower indices. Consequently
∇T​Sa=∂λ​∂μ​xa+Γabc​SbTc=∇S​Ta.
(90)
Using this equality and the supplied curvature-commutator convention,
∇T2​S=∇T​∇S​T=∇S​∇T​T+[∇T​,∇S​]T=R(T,S)T.
(91)
In components the geodesic deviation equation is
∇T2​Sa=Rabcd​TbTcSd.​
(92)
It describes the relative acceleration of nearby freely falling worldlines. A freely falling observer can remove the connection at an event by choosing a local inertial frame, but cannot remove the curvature-dependent tidal acceleration of neighboring freely falling particles. Measuring their separation and relative acceleration therefore measures the local gravitational tidal field.

The lubrication approximation requires depth h small compared with the horizontal variation scale L, small bottom slopes, and negligible inertia on the scale ρUh2/(μL)≪1. Treat the prescribed flat surface as steady and impermeable to leading order. The leading Stokes equations give pz​=0 and μ∂z2​uH​=∇H​p. No slip at z=−h and the imposed shear μ∂z​uH​∣0​=S yield
uH​(z)=2μz2−h2​∇H​p+μz+h​S.
(93)
Integration and depth-integrated incompressibility now give
∇H​⋅q=0,μq=−3h3​∇H​p+2h2​S.​
(94)
The surface value is u0​=−h2∇H​p/(2μ)+hS/μ. Eliminate the pressure gradient with the flux relation to obtain
u0​=2h3q​+4μhS​.​
(95)
For the circular container, write q=∇ψ×z^=(ψy​,−ψx​). Curl the relation μq/h3=−∇p/3+S/(2h) for S=(S0​,0). Its vertical component gives
∇⋅(h3∇ψ​)=−2μh2S0​​hy​.​
(96)
The wall condition q⋅n=0 says ψ is constant on the boundary; choose that constant zero. If h=h0​, the equation is Laplace's equation with zero Dirichlet data. The strong maximum principle for harmonic functions gives ψ=0 and q=0, though there is a sheared return flow through the depth. Its surface velocity is u0​=(h0​S0​/(4μ),0)​.
For h=h0​(1+εy/a), the first-order equation is h0−3​Δψ=−εS0​/(2μh0​a)+O(ε2). The zero-boundary quadratic solution is
ψ=εC(x2+y2−a2)+O(ε2),C=−8μaS0​h02​​.​
(97)
Thus q=2εC(y,−x)+O(ε2). Inserting this and the varying depth into the surface formula gives
u0​=4μS0​h0​​(1−2aεy​, 2a3εx​)+O(ε2).​
(98)
The circulation is first order in the bottom slope, while its wall-normal flux remains zero.

37B OurBigBook.com
For isentropic flow of a perfect gas, p=Kργ with γ>1 and c2=dp/dρ. The mass and momentum equations imply
ct​+ucx​+2γ−1​cux​=0,ut​+uux​+γ−12c​cx​=0.
(99)
Adding and subtracting the appropriate multiples therefore proves
[∂t​+(u±c)∂x​][u±γ−12(c−c0​)​]=0.​
(100)
These are the Riemann invariants for one-dimensional isentropic flow.
In the piston-driven rarefaction wave, the incoming minus invariant has its initial value zero. Thus c=c0​+(γ−1)u/2. At the piston up​=−ft, giving cp​=c0​−(γ−1)ft/2. A plus characteristic emitted at time τ has constant u=−fτ and c=c0​−(γ−1)fτ/2, so its straight trajectory is
x(t;τ)=−21​fτ2+[c0​−2γ+1​fτ](t−τ).
(101)
The first characteristic is x=c0​t, ahead of which the gas is undisturbed. Later characteristics have decreasing propagation speed and spread into a rarefaction. More explicitly ∂τ​x=−c0​−(γ+1)ft/2+γfτ<0 for τ≤t<tv​, with equality only at the vacuum endpoint. They never intersect, so no compressive shock forms.
Since p/p0​=(c/c0​)2γ/(γ−1), the vacuum formation at an accelerating withdrawing piston gives
pp​(t)=p0​(1−t/tv​)2γ/(γ−1)(0≤t<tv​),tv​=f(γ−1)2c0​​.​
(102)
At tv​, density, sound speed and pressure at the gas edge vanish, and the piston velocity is X˙(tv​)=−2c0​/(γ−1)​. Its speed is the positive magnitude 2c0​/(γ−1). Afterwards the gas edge continues at this limiting velocity, while the piston keeps accelerating away; a vacuum gap of width f(t−tv​)2/2 opens and the gas pressure on the piston stays zero.

Substitute the exact smooth solution into the leapfrog advection scheme and expand the centered differences. With τ=Δt and h=Δx, the normalized local truncation error is
2τu(x,t+τ)−u(x,t−τ)​−2hu(x+h,t)−u(x−h,t)​=6τ2​uttt​−6h2​uxxx​+O(τ4+h4).
(103)
Because ut​=ux​, repeated differentiation gives uttt​=uxxx​. Hence
T=6τ2−h2​uxxx​+O(τ4+h4).​
(104)
Equivalently the unnormalized one-update residual is τ(τ2−h2)uxxx​/3+O(τ5+τh4). Thus the scheme is second order in space and time. When τ=h, the exact translating solution u(x,t)=F(x+t) satisfies the grid recurrence exactly; initialization still matters for the independent computational branch.

b

Words: 163 Articles: 1
38C OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 163
b OurBigBook.com
Insert the Fourier mode umn​=gneimθ into the leapfrog advection scheme. The amplification roots satisfy
g2−2iμsinθg−1=0,g±​=iμsinθ±1−μ2sin2θ​.
(105)
For 0<μ<1, both roots have modulus one and remain uniformly separated by at least 21−μ2​. The two-level Fourier amplification matrices are therefore uniformly diagonalizable, and their powers stay bounded. The Parseval identity gives stability in the discrete two-norm. For μ>1, some frequencies have ∣μsinθ∣>1 and one root has modulus greater than one, giving instability.
For two-level stability at the leapfrog Courant boundary, at μ=1 and θ=π/2, the repeated root is i and the recurrence has solutions an​=(A+Bn)in. For example a0​=0,a1​=1 gives an​=nin−1. Thus arbitrary two-level perturbations grow without a uniform power bound. The precise answer for unrestricted starting data is
0<μ<1 is stable;μ>1 is unstable;μ=1 is a repeated-root boundary case.​
(106)
The often-used root-modulus CFL condition is μ≤1, but by itself it misses this boundary Jordan growth. A startup that selects the exact translating branch at μ=1 removes that growth for the selected data; it does not make the unrestricted two-level update power-bounded.
